name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,177

clue.text: When travelling, grandma tours one American high street

indicators.note: a traveller moves about, so these letters are on the move into a new order
to tour a place is to go all round it, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A globetrotting grandmother visits a single American shopping street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tours' reads as sightseeing, but it puts the numeral inside the jumbled letters. Main drag is North American slang, unfamiliar to many British solvers.
explanation.definitionFit: In North American slang the main drag is a town's principal thoroughfare, equivalent to the British high street.

clue.text: Fairly new part of leisure centre

indicators.note: only a portion of the following words is used, so the letters sit inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Describing a newly built section of a sports complex.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the word break: leisuRE CENTre.
explanation.definitionFit: Something recent happened or appeared not long ago, which is a plain synonym for being fairly new.

clue.text: Prediction on behalf of English players

blocks.note: doing something for someone is acting on their behalf
standard abbreviation for English
the players in a production are its cast

explanation.surface: A pundit forecasting results for the England team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players' suggests sport, but here it means actors, the cast of a show.
explanation.definitionFit: A forecast is a statement of what is expected to happen, the same thing as a prediction.

clue.text: One securing bank of stadium seats

blocks.note: first meaning: someone who ties things fast
second meaning: one level of rows in a stand

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a whimsical agent noun from the verb 'tie', pronounced differently from the seating sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A tier is a raised row or level of seating, and a person who ties knots is literally a tie-er.

clue.text: Part of drain clogged in the middle, say

definitions.note: playful description, not a dictionary sense

blocks.note: first meaning: the channel along a roof or road that carries water to the drains
second, whimsical meaning: something with its gut, its middle, stopped up

explanation.surface: A plumber's report on a blocked section of pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a jokey reading: the gut is the body's middle, so a 'gut-ter' is a thing troubled there; 'say' flags the liberty taken.
explanation.definitionFit: A gutter is the trough that channels rainwater into a drainage system, one component of the whole drain.

clue.text: Make endlessly healthy food

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: a make of car is the manufacturer's trade name

explanation.surface: An instruction to keep cooking nutritious dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make' reads as a verb but is the noun meaning a manufacturer's label.
explanation.definitionFit: Bran, the husks of cereal grain, is eaten for its fibre and is a classic example of a health food.

clue.text: Take out fruit

blocks.note: first meaning: to go out romantically with someone
second meaning: the sweet fruit of a palm tree

explanation.walkthrough: 'Take out' tempts as removal or deletion, but it is the romantic sense of escorting someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To date someone is to take them out socially, and the date palm bears a sticky brown fruit.

clue.text: Passing remarks?

blocks.note: surface reading: casual comments made in passing
setter's reading: words written about someone's passing, that is their death

explanation.walkthrough: 'Passing' is a euphemism for dying, so the remarks are those published about the deceased.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper notice recounting a dead person's life is written on the occasion of their death, their passing.

clue.text: Addendum to document provided by McCann execs

indicators.note: the letters are supplied from within the following words themselves

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: Executives at the McCann advertising agency draft an appendix to a contract.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the words: McCANN EXEcs.
explanation.definitionFit: An annexe is a supplementary section attached to a report or treaty, the same as an addendum.

clue.text: Stout bar surrounding barrel

indicators.note: to surround something is to enclose it, so one piece sits around another

blocks.note: a rod is a bar of metal or wood
a tun is a large cask

explanation.surface: A pub where stout is served from a barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout' and 'bar' suggest beer in a pub; stout is the adjective for a portly person and the bar is a metal rod.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotund describes a plump, round-bodied person, exactly what stout means when used of build.

clue.text: Rubbish is, in the first instance, going to decay

indicators.note: the first instance is the very start, so only an opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
to rot is to decay

explanation.surface: An observation that household waste starts decomposing early.
explanation.walkthrough: Grot is informal British slang for rubbish or junk.
explanation.definitionFit: Grot is a British colloquial word for unpleasant junk or dirt, a slang synonym for rubbish.

clue.text: Get a role playing intimate friend

indicators.note: letters at play are moved about freely, so they take a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An actor lands a part portraying the hero's best friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing' and 'role' make a theatrical scene, but 'playing' is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides a second self, alter ego can mean a trusted close companion, like a second version of oneself.

clue.text: What takes a toll on America? Go Fish

definitions.text: What takes a toll on America?

blocks.note: your go in a game is your turn
the pike is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A question about what harms the US, answered by the card game Go Fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes a toll on' usually means harms; here it is literal, a road that charges a toll. Go Fish looks like a single card-game name.
explanation.definitionFit: In the United States a turnpike is a highway on which drivers pay a fee, so it collects tolls.

clue.text: Girl ran, ran fast

blocks.note: gal is an informal word for a girl
loped means ran with long easy strides

explanation.surface: A girl who ran and ran quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'ran' reads as emphasis, but the first is wordplay and the second starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To gallop is to move at the fastest pace, like a horse at full speed, so galloped means sped along.

clue.text: Sparkly silver items thoughtlessly dropped?

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
litter is rubbish carelessly discarded

explanation.surface: Shiny silver trinkets someone has absent-mindedly let fall.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the second part as a definition by description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Aglitter is a literary adjective for glittering, shining with bright flashes of light, the same as sparkly.

clue.text: Entirely enthusiastic about toys with 50 per cent off

indicators.note: a half-price reduction removes half, so half the letters are dropped

blocks.note: being into something means being keen on it
taken as written before being halved

explanation.surface: A shopper thrilled about a half-price toy sale.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half of the four letters survives. In toto is Latin for completely.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase in toto, borrowed into English, means as a whole or completely, a synonym for entirely.

clue.text: Spring festival primarily hosted on Long Island

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letters are kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A spring celebration being staged mainly in New York's Long Island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primarily' looks like 'mainly', but it takes initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Holi is the Hindu festival of colours celebrated each year in March, marking the arrival of spring.

clue.text: What may be used in cultivating privileged pupils here

definitions.text: What may be used in cultivating

blocks.clueFragment: What may be used in cultivating
blocks.note: first meaning: a farm implement for breaking up soil
second meaning: a famous fee-paying English school

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cultivating privileged pupils' reads as educating an elite; cultivating is the farming sense. Harrow is an expensive private boarding school near London.
explanation.definitionFit: A harrow is a spiked frame dragged over ploughed land, and Harrow School educates wealthy boys in northwest London.

clue.text: Mechanic ultimately has favourable opinion of battered cars

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
to rate someone is to think well of them

explanation.surface: A mechanic who, in the end, quite likes beaten-up old cars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' reads as 'in the end, after all', but it takes the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Crate is informal slang for an old, dilapidated vehicle, so crates are worn-out, battered cars.

clue.text: Bird heading away from stream

indicators.note: the head of a word is its start, so its first letter goes

blocks.note: a brook is a small stream

explanation.surface: A bird flying off from a creek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading away' reads as flying off, but it removes the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The rook is a black, crow-like bird found across Europe, nesting in colonies called rookeries.

clue.text: Hands over change

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: paws is informal for hands

explanation.surface: Someone handing over loose coins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands over' looks like a phrasal verb, but it is the hands word followed by the turning signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To swap is to exchange one thing for another, which is one meaning of the verb change.

clue.text: A child’s party?

blocks.note: per means 'a' as in 'two pounds a head'
a son is a male child

explanation.surface: A question about a children's birthday party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' suggests a celebration, but it is the legal sense of one person involved in a matter.
explanation.definitionFit: In legal and formal usage a party is an individual involved in a contract or dispute, so a person.

clue.text: Frank blog entry with influence

blocks.note: a single entry on a blog is a post
to leave a mark is to have an influence

explanation.surface: An honest blog post written by an influencer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' reads as candid, describing the blog; it is the noun for the stamp on mail.
explanation.definitionFit: A frank is the official stamp on mail showing postage is paid, the same thing as a postmark.

clue.text: Is required to pay co-owners on a regular basis

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so every second letter is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: Joint owners who have to make payments regularly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On a regular basis' reads as recurring payments; it picks alternate letters, ignoring the hyphen.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who owes money has a debt and is therefore obliged to pay it back.
